cls: Topical decapeptide / basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF)-related peptide
quick: 0.1% topical solution applied to depigmented lesions, usually once or twice daily
Safety not established - use with caution / physician advice
Not applicable - topical, no systemic clearance concern
Clinical repigmentation response and local tolerability
summary: Deca Peptide is a topical basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF)-related decapeptide (a 10-amino-acid peptide), marketed in India (e.g. Melgain, DCGI-approved since around 2004) as a 0.1% solution and used as an ADJUVANT in stable vitiligo to promote repigmentation - chiefly in combination with phototherapy (NBUVB/PUVA), topical tacrolimus or corticosteroids. It is thought to act like bFGF, a melanocyte mitogen, stimulating proliferation and migration of melanocytes into depigmented skin. It is generally very well tolerated, with at most mild local irritation. It is NOT an FDA-approved drug; the supporting evidence is limited and largely from small, open-label Indian studies, and there are essentially no authoritative pharmacokinetic, pregnancy, or overdose data. Marketing claims for hair growth and anti-ageing are weakly substantiated.
indications: Adjuvant treatment of stable vitiligo to promote repigmentation (chiefly combined with phototherapy or topical immunomodulators)
Marketed (weakly substantiated) for hair growth and skin/anti-ageing use

dosage.d: 0.1% topical solution applied to depigmented lesions; label suggests bedtime application followed by short morning sun exposure (~10-15 min)
dosage.n: Most effective combined with NBUVB/PUVA, tacrolimus 0.1% or topical steroids; response is slow (months up to ~1 year)

admin: For topical, external use only on affected (depigmented) lesions
Apply per label - commonly at bedtime, with short controlled sun/phototherapy exposure as directed
Often used as an adjuvant alongside phototherapy or topical immunomodulators
moa: The peptide relates to / mimics basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), a melanocyte mitogen. Vitiligo is associated with melanocyte growth-factor deprivation; the decapeptide is thought to stimulate proliferation and migration of melanocytes (with increased phosphorylated focal adhesion kinase expression), driving repigmentation from lesion margins and follicular reservoirs. Phototherapy synergises by inducing keratinocytes to release endogenous bFGF.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to the peptide or any excipient
relative: Pregnancy and lactation (safety not established - use with caution)
monitor: Clinical degree of repigmentation over time

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established; data are limited. Labeling advises caution and physician consultation in pregnancy.
lact: Safety during breastfeeding is not established; caution or avoidance is advised due to limited data.
renal: Not applicable - topical agent with no documented systemic clearance concerns.
hepatic: Not applicable - topical agent with no documented systemic clearance concerns.

minor: Commonly and intentionally co-used (synergistically) with NBUVB/PUVA phototherapy, tacrolimus or topical corticosteroids

rare: Local skin irritation, dryness, transient erythema or burning at the application site (usually mild and self-limiting)
emergency: Signs of a local hypersensitivity reaction (marked irritation or rash)

monitoring: Clinical assessment of repigmentation (degree/grade) over months
counsel: This is a topical solution used to help colour return to white (vitiligo) patches, usually alongside light therapy
Repigmentation is slow - it can take many months, sometimes up to a year
It works best when combined with phototherapy or other prescribed creams, not on its own
Apply only to the affected skin as directed; mild stinging or dryness can occur
It is a cosmeceutical/adjuvant with limited evidence and is not FDA-approved
pk: Not characterised - acts locally on lesional melanocytes
Not characterised - systemic pharmacokinetics essentially unstudied
Local action; sustained use required for ongoing effect
pearls: An adjuvant cosmeceutical peptide for STABLE vitiligo - not a standalone cure
Works best combined with phototherapy (NBUVB/PUVA) or tacrolimus/steroids, which consistently outperform monotherapy
Response is slow (months up to ~1 year); generally very well tolerated
Thought to act like bFGF, stimulating melanocyte proliferation and migration
DCGI-approved in India (~2004); NOT FDA-approved, with limited and largely open-label evidence and essentially no PK/pregnancy/overdose data
missed: If an application is missed, apply it when remembered and resume the usual schedule; do not double-apply. Consistent regular use is needed for benefit.
overdose: Not applicable - topical agent; no systemic overdose is expected. Manage any local reaction symptomatically.
